responseText:
Good question — they sound similar but have different effects depending on your role and the calendar system. High-level differences:

- Purpose
  - Cancel: The organizer ends the meeting for everyone and notifies invited attendees that it will not happen.
  - Delete: Removes the event from a single calendar (usually your own). It does not inherently communicate a cancellation to other attendees.

- Who should do it
  - Organizer: Should cancel (so everyone is informed and any resources are released).
  - Attendee: Typically deletes from their personal calendar if they no longer want the entry; they should RSVP “Decline” or ask the organizer to cancel if the meeting itself should stop.

- Notifications and updates
  - Cancel: Generates a cancellation notice/update that is sent to all guests (so their calendars are updated and the meeting is removed or marked canceled).
  - Delete: If you delete an event you received, most systems simply remove it from your calendar without sending a cancellation to others. If an organizer deletes without sending cancellation, other guests may still have the event on their calendars.

- Effect on conferencing/rooms/resources
  - Cancel: Frees booked resources (meeting rooms, conference bridges) and typically updates those reservations.
  - Delete: Removing a local copy does not release resources reserved by the organizer.

- Recurring events
  - Cancel: Organizer can cancel one occurrence or the whole series; cancellation propagates to all invitees accordingly.
  - Delete: An attendee deleting one occurrence or the series only affects their view; an organizer deleting a series should normally send cancellation to guests to remove it everywhere.

- Audit/record-keeping and visibility
  - Cancel: Leaves a trace (a cancellation message) in attendees’ mailboxes/calendars; is explicit and auditable.
  - Delete: May leave no trace for other participants; only affects the calendar where the delete was performed.

- Etiquette and best practice
  - If you organized the meeting and it will not happen, cancel it so everyone knows and resources are freed.
  - If you’re just removing clutter from your own schedule, delete it locally (or decline the invite) — but if the meeting needs to stop for all, ask the organizer to cancel.

- Platform-specific behavior
  - Exact behavior varies by calendar system (Google Calendar, Outlook/Exchange, Apple Calendar). Most common pattern: organizer-triggered cancellation notifies guests; attendee deletion is local. Always check the prompts your calendar shows when deleting (many apps ask whether to notify guests).

Short summary: cancel = stop the meeting for everyone and notify; delete = remove from a calendar (usually your own) and usually does not notify others.
